title: A Mysterious Rash of Star Birth
caption: The Fireworks Galaxy, NGC 6946, imaged by the Gemini North telescope

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Pink bubbles of glowing hydrogen are scattered across the arms of NGC 6946, a spiral galaxy seen face-on in this sharp Gemini North image. Each pink patch is gas lit by hot, massive young stars, whose ultraviolet radiation makes the surrounding clouds glow red.

For reasons nobody yet understands, NGC 6946 forms stars at a much higher rate than any of the other large galaxies in our local neighbourhood. Because massive stars live short lives and end as supernovae, all that star birth means the galaxy has seen explosions in rapid succession for tens of millions of years.

Eight supernovae are known to have exploded in its arms over the past century, making it the most prolific known galaxy for supernovae in that time and earning it the nickname the Fireworks Galaxy. If a million years of its history were squeezed into a few seconds of film, it would show an almost constant flicker of new stars flaring into view and old ones dying.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with GMOS on Gemini North through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published for this image.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red glow of hydrogen, so star-forming regions stand out far more than they would to the eye.

explore: NGC 6946 lies about 20 million light-years away, according to the caption. The image was taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on Gemini North, on Mauna Kea in Hawai'i, and covers about 5.80 by 5.58 arcminutes of sky.
alt: A face-on spiral galaxy whose arms are dotted with pink bubbles of glowing hydrogen gas.
